16687: In Philippi, Paul met a slave girl who had a 'spirit of python' and earned her owners money by fortune-telling. 16688: According to Greek myth, the serpent (or dragon) Python guarded the ancient oracle at Pytho, later called Delphi. The young god Apollo killed it with his arrows and took over the oracle, which was then delivered through his priestess, the Pythia. The Pythian Games commemorated the victory. By the Roman era, 'python' had also become a popular word for someone who spoke oracles from inside themselves; Plutarch (*On the Obsolescence of Oracles* 9) notes that ventriloquists were then called 'pythons'.
16689:
Luke writes that the girl had *pneuma pythōna*, literally 'a spirit, a python' (Acts 16:16). Older translations soften this to 'a spirit of divination'. For several days she followed Paul's group crying, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who show us the way of salvation' (Acts 16:17). Her words were true, but Paul, 'greatly annoyed', commanded the spirit in the name of Jesus Christ to come out, and it left 'that very hour' (Acts 16:18). Her owners, seeing their profit gone, dragged Paul and Silas to the magistrates, who had them beaten and imprisoned (Acts 16:19-24) — leading to the earthquake and the jailer's conversion.

Luke presents the spirit as a real power, not a trick, while treating its source as unclean. The Old Testament had already forbidden divination and consulting mediums (Deut 18:10-12); the Greek translation uses *engastrimythos* ('belly-talker') for the medium at Endor (1 Sam 28:7), the same kind of figure later called a 'python'.

16720: The golden calf was a bull image made twice in Israel's story: once by Aaron at Mount Sinai, and again centuries later by King Jeroboam, who set up two calves at Bethel and Dan. Both times the people were told, 'Here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt.' The striking thing is that the calf was not presented as a foreign god but as a way of worshipping Israel's own God — which is exactly what the Bible condemns.
16721: There is no myth of the calf itself. In the ancient Near East the young bull was a common symbol of strength and fertility and was linked with gods such as El ('Bull El' at Ugarit) and the storm god Baal-Hadad, who was often shown standing on a bull. Gods were frequently pictured riding or standing on animals, so a bull could be an image of a god or a pedestal for an invisible one.
16722:
**At Sinai.** While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to 'make us gods (elohim) who shall go before us'. He melts their gold earrings and makes a calf; they say, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.' Aaron builds an altar and announces, 'Tomorrow is a feast to the LORD (Yahweh)' (Exod 32:1-6). Moses breaks the tablets, burns and grinds the calf, scatters it on water and makes the people drink it (Exod 32:19-20). The Levites kill about three thousand (Exod 32:28). Israel later remembers this as its defining apostasy: 'they exchanged their glory for the image of an ox that eats grass' (Ps 106:19-20; Deut 9:16; Neh 9:18; Acts 7:41).

**Jeroboam's calves.** When the kingdom split (c. 930 BC), Jeroboam feared his people would return to Jerusalem's temple. He made two golden calves, put one in Bethel and one in Dan, and used the same words: 'Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt' (1 Kgs 12:28-30). He appointed non-Levite priests and a new festival (1 Kgs 12:31-33). From then on, 'the sin of Jeroboam' is the standard by which Kings judges every northern king (for example 2 Kgs 10:29; 2 Kgs 17:21-22). Hosea mocks: 'Men who sacrifice kiss calves!' (Hos 13:2; Hos 8:5-6).

**What were the calves?** Three main views:
1. **Pedestal view** (W. F. Albright and many since): the calves were thrones or mounts for the invisible Yahweh, like the cherubim of the ark. The sin was making an image that blurred into idolatry.
2. **Image of Yahweh**: the calf represented Yahweh himself in bull form, against the command not to make images of God (Exod 20:4).
3. **Foreign influence**: the calf copied the Egyptian Apis or Hathor (Sinai) or the Canaanite El/Baal bull (Bethel). Jeroboam had spent time in Egypt (1 Kgs 11:40).
Many scholars combine 1 and 3. Many also suspect that the Sinai story was written or shaped with Jeroboam's calves in view, because of the identical slogan; traditional readers take the Sinai event as historical and Jeroboam as deliberately reviving it. Debated.
16724: A 'feast to the LORD' around a golden calf breaks the covenant just made. Moses intercedes and the people are spared destruction, but judgement falls.

16756: Nehushtan was the bronze serpent Moses made in the wilderness so that people bitten by snakes could look at it and live. Israel kept it for about five hundred years, until people were burning incense to it. King Hezekiah smashed it and called it Nehushtan — roughly 'that bronze thing'. Jesus later compared his own lifting up on the cross to the serpent on the pole.
16757: Nehushtan has no myth outside the Bible. Snake imagery was widespread and ambiguous in the ancient Near East: serpents could be deadly enemies (like the Egyptian chaos-serpent Apophis) or protective and healing (like the Egyptian uraeus cobra, or later the snake of the Greek healing god Asclepius). Winged serpents called seraphim appear on Judahite seals of the 8th century BC.
16758:
**In the wilderness.** When Israel complains against God and Moses, 'fiery serpents' (seraphim) bite the people and many die. When they confess, God tells Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole; anyone bitten who looks at it lives. Moses makes a serpent of bronze (Num 21:4-9). The healing comes from God's promise, not the metal.

**In the temple.** Centuries later, Hezekiah 'broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan' (2 Kgs 18:4). An object once used by God became an idol because people treated it as a source of power in itself.

**In the New Testament.** Jesus tells Nicodemus, 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life' (John 3:14-15). Paul uses the serpent episode as a warning against testing Christ (1 Cor 10:9).

**Scholarly questions.** Some historians think the temple serpent was originally a Canaanite or Egyptian-style healing emblem, and that the Num 21 story explained its presence; others accept the story as the true origin. Whether Hezekiah coined the name or it was already in use is also debated.
16760: In the wilderness, God provides healing through a bronze serpent on a pole. The cure requires only looking in trust.

16787: Teraphim were household god-images kept in family homes, used for protection and for asking guidance. Rachel stole her father Laban's teraphim; Michal used one to fool Saul's soldiers; and the prophets condemned teraphim as useless. They show that ordinary family religion in Israel often mixed devotion to Yahweh with other practices.
16788: There is no myth. The meaning of the word is debated: suggestions include a link to the Rephaim (the dead ancestors), to a Hittite word *tarpi* (a spirit), or to a root meaning 'decay', used mockingly ('rotten things'). Many scholars today think teraphim were images of deceased ancestors consulted for guidance, but this is not certain.
16789:
**Rachel and Laban.** As Jacob's family secretly leaves Haran, Rachel steals her father's teraphim. Laban pursues them, calling them 'my gods'. Rachel hides them in a camel saddle, sits on them and says she cannot get up because 'the way of women' is upon her (Gen 31:19; Gen 31:30-35). The scene ridicules the 'gods' — they are sat on by a supposedly unclean woman. Later Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods, and buries them at Shechem (Gen 35:2-4).

**Michal and David.** Michal lets David escape through a window and puts the teraphim in his bed with goat hair at its head to deceive Saul's messengers (1 Sam 19:11-16). That a teraphim was in David's house at all is striking.

**Micah and the Danites.** In Judges, Micah of Ephraim makes an ephod and teraphim for his private shrine; the tribe of Dan steals them and his priest for their new city (Judg 17:5; Judg 18:14-20).

**Condemnation and divination.** Samuel equates stubbornness with 'iniquity and teraphim' (1 Sam 15:23). Josiah removes them in his reform (2 Kgs 23:24). Ezekiel says the king of Babylon 'consulted the teraphim' at a crossroads (Ezek 21:21), and Zechariah says 'the teraphim have spoken vanity' (Zech 10:2). Hosea lists teraphim with ephod and pillar among things Israel will be without during exile (Hos 3:4), a puzzling verse that some read as neutral.

**Why did Rachel steal them?** Older scholarship (from Cyrus Gordon in the 1930s) cited the Nuzi tablets to argue that holding the household gods gave a claim to the family inheritance. Later studies (Moshe Greenberg, 1962, and others) weakened this reading. Other suggestions: for protection on the journey, to stop Laban divining where they went, or simple devotion. Debated.
16791: Laban searches the tents for his household gods; Rachel sits on them. The story mocks gods that cannot protect themselves.

16821: Gad and Meni were gods of Luck and Destiny. In Isaiah, God condemns those who 'set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny'. The prophet then turns the word for destiny into a pun: 'I will destine you to the sword.'
16822: There are no myths. 'Gad' was a common Semitic word for good fortune, and the god Gad was a personified luck-spirit, often the protecting fortune of a person or city, similar to the Greek Tyche. Meni is less well known; some scholars connect it with Manat, a pre-Islamic Arabian goddess of fate, but the link is uncertain.
16823:
Isaiah addresses those 'who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Gad and fill cups of mixed wine for Meni' (Isa 65:11). The next verse plays on the second name: 'I will destine (maniti) you to the sword' (Isa 65:12). The point: if you trust in Destiny, God will give you a destiny — just not the one you hoped for. The KJV translated the names as common nouns, 'that troop' and 'that number', which hides the gods. Modern translations print Fortune and Destiny or Gad and Meni.

The word gad also appears in names. When Leah's maid bore a son, Leah said 'Good fortune comes!' and named him Gad (Gen 30:11). Places such as Baal-gad (Josh 11:17) and Migdal-gad (Josh 15:37) show the word in religious and place names. Whether these refer to the deity or just to 'luck' is debated.

16851: On the Day of Atonement, Israel's high priest cast lots over two goats: one 'for the LORD', sacrificed as a sin offering, and one 'for Azazel', sent alive into the wilderness carrying the people's sins. Nobody is sure what Azazel means. It may be the name of a desert demon, the name of a place, or a word meaning 'complete removal'.
16852: The Bible tells no story about Azazel. Later Jewish writings do. In *1 Enoch* (3rd-2nd century BC), Asael (Azazel in later copies) is one of the rebel angels, the Watchers, who taught humans to make weapons, jewellery and cosmetics; God orders the angel Raphael to bind him hand and foot and throw him into darkness in the desert under jagged rocks until the judgement (1 Enoch 8:1; 10:4-8). This links the Day of Atonement goat with the angels of Gen 6. In the *Apocalypse of Abraham* (1st-2nd century AD), Azazel is an unclean bird and the tempter. A Qumran text (4Q180) also refers to Azazel and the angels.
